Today the air around me feels thick with forgotten syllables, like a book left open on a windowsill that collects dust in the corners of its pages. I sit, a solitary figure huddled over a folded piece of paper—a kind of talisman that holds promise, that looks like it might pull together threads of life into tidy, predictable sentences. The world beyond the front‑door is a deep blue, a horizon that never quite unblinks no matter how many times I stare at it. I remember the first time I tried to walk across a backyard fence and the last time I stepped onto a boat, testing the cold water like a litmus paper for courage. The memory is hazy and bright at once, a person’s childhood sigh weaving ivy around its edges.

When I look outward, it feels like an endless corridor of time, and in that corridor my footsteps echo like drums that became startled down the floorboards of a house that once belonged to a grandmother who liked to speak in riddles. The things that lie between the seconds feel like cells in a body; the bodies can be filled with invisible forces, the pressure that kept us in that house in the 1960s, the echo of a wedding laugh that bounced off the walls when the guests left with a clink of a glass. I want to step back into that original space and feel the deliberate traffic of that scene, but the continents of memory keep on changing form as if they are conscious. You cannot catch a particular speech or picture and hold on. That is the great paradox of remembering a favorite coffee that was freshly brewed at the attic table where the scent rose in steam‑shaped small spirals. That coffee in the memory burns and sometimes turns to ash because I am craving something else.

Blends of sounds hover around me, a diurnal orchestra? I hear the hum of a refrigerator that meets only the dejection of a bruise and the soft shrieks of a kitchen demon who likes to scorn cleanliness. The texture of city streets at dawn is a separate little toy in my mind. Even as I write, the crunch of wet leaves against the asphalt glows in the grayscale. Let me be the narrator of the sensory world: the sharp taste of a lemon, with its acidic perfume that can whiten my inner thoughts. Mixing the oppressive hotness of the summer’s blank café with the sting of a wintere cold. It is not just tedium. It is the discovery of myself in written form, absorbing every detail like a filament that glows.

I notice myself attempting to turn these feelings and memories into a poem or a slice of reality, making the page in which they live for a day. There's a peculiar way in which the words keep becoming something heavier than the physical weight of the paper on my desk. Maybe they are thoughts, or maybe they are ghosts that want to pick me up and let the world ask a question: “How do you see it?” Each question is a grain of sedimentism, taken and soaked, turned toward a radiative verve in the building a brick of writing. I recall living in a room with a small armchair that claims to feed the world with stories just by absorbing each inhale and exhale. So my heart takes an odd sort of cruelty into the thing like these are the only times I have not owned my narrative before I lived.

At the end, I don't really know if I'm looking in. That is what the world is worth: a labyrinth of sounds. The one thing that remains is the arch that I wish to be as strong as the one I had at the cusp of first love. There's a sense of wonder in the small arc of the repository I made. I see the faintest of lines that would tie everything into a shape. The same place where I know that sometimes food may taste but is also a source of hope, a free vehicle of life encouraging new birth. The world has to rest a little in a crack, letting in the bright tomorrow from a simple sketch of a bird.

When I finish this, whatever comes next—whatever I will consider, I will think of as how the words sometimes seem to bleed through and leave beyond the page. That is what it all means to me: The fact that these 1000 words are not just markers or numbers, but a space that I as a writer or reader can mine, carry, and keep seeping in. The question is what do I not know about myself? I chime into the quiet of the tears and hope that the tangible moment of silence might have a bigger secret than I can ever find. The other side of forgetting is that we still never end. I will hang up the final line on the wall of my mind in the hopes that it might catch a light and shine.
